visible.summary:
Romania is broadly workable with a conservative political climate and significant legal-protection gaps, but a landmark EU court ruling and active civil society provide some positive trajectory. The European Court of Justice ruled in 2024 that Romania must recognize gender-identity changes made in other EU member states (the Mirin case), and a Romanian court definitively confirmed this in March 2026. Bucharest Pride marked its 20th anniversary with tens of thousands of marchers.

However, domestic legal gender recognition is court-based, restrictive, and inconsistently implemented. The anti-discrimination law does not explicitly cover gender identity (it covers "sex" and "sexual orientation" only), and the hate-crime law's aggravating-circumstance provision has never been applied in SOGIESC cases. No same-sex marriage or civil unions are recognised (the Orthodox Church successfully opposed reform). Far-right influences rose during the 2024-2025 election cycle, with anti-LGBTI rhetoric "intensified and repeatedly instrumentalised for political mobilisation."

For a visitor: EU/Schengen, no trans-specific border friction, no criminalisation, bathrooms unrestricted. The ECJ ruling means EU-issued LGR documents must be recognised.
visible.tangentialFactors: No same-sex marriage or civil unions recognised — relevant to trans visitors travelling with partners.
visible.localsOnly: The court-based domestic LGR regime and its inconsistent implementation are resident-facing; the ECJ Mirin ruling directly benefits EU-recognised trans visitors' documents.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: No trans-specific travel advisory; general urban crime is moderate.

sources.claim: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying Reuters report (Oct 2024) covers the CJEU ruling that Romania infringed a transgender man's rights (the Mirzarafie-Ahi case on recognition of UK gender recognition).

ACCEPT Romania (31 Mar 2026): the Sector 6 Court of Bucharest ordered a new birth certificate for trans man Arian Mirzarafie-Ahi reflecting his UK-recognised identity, and the ruling became definitive after the Bucharest Tribunal rejected appeals filed by the Cluj civil-status directorates — building on the CJEU's 2024 ruling that member states must transcribe intra-EU legal gender recognition. Announced on Trans Day of Visibility; ACCEPT urges others who changed documents in another EU country to pursue transcription in Romania.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2026 (covering Jan–Dec 2025): anti-LGBTI rhetoric intensified during the 2025 presidential campaign — candidate Călin Georgescu declared himself 'against LGBTQ' in February and PM Ciolacu mocked gender-marker changes; the National Audiovisual Council issued a public warning to B1 TV in August over anti-Pride 'provocation' framing after an ACCEPT complaint; a Ploiești deputy mayor of AUR made further derogatory announcements.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023): the CNCD investigated printing houses that refused to print LGBT and gender-equality materials; the IPSOS PRIDE 2023 survey found 51% of Romanians agree same-sex families should enjoy legal recognition; March 2024 education-law drafts carried anti-discrimination provisions that drew 13 religious groups' protests and a 50+ organisation counter-response.

Outright International Romania overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex relations legal nationwide; GO 137/2000 covers sex and sexual orientation but institutional follow-through is limited; no marriage or civil unions (the 2018 constitution-ban referendum failed on low turnout; the Orthodox Church has opposed a civil-partnership bill since 2017); legal gender recognition possible; LGBTI organisations can register.

Council of Europe thematic review (Jan 2023): 'Hate Crimes and Other Hate Motivated Incidents Against LGBTI People in Romania' - national report on implementation of Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)5, covering legal/policy frameworks, applicable ECtHR case-law and international standards.

ILGA-Europe and partners' submission to the EU 2025 Rule of Law Report (2025), with ACCEPT Romania authoring the Romania chapter (p.29): of nine country submissions, eight reported smear campaigns, disinformation and hate speech against LGBTI people — the surge in anti-LGBTI narratives during the Romanian election period is cited as the clearest example of rights-impacting rule-of-law erosion.
AP (Jun 2025): 'Bucharest gay pride march turns 20 as LGBTQ+ Romanians face growing hostility' — tens of thousands march on the 20th anniversary amid rising right-wing hostility.

FRA-commissioned legal study (Feb 2008) by Romanița Elena Iordache and Iustina Ionescu: maps how Romanian law implemented the EU Employment Directive 2000/78/EC and free-movement rules for LGBT partners — national anti-discrimination concepts, CNCD enforcement powers and NGO complaints; a dated baseline for Romania's protection architecture.

visible.summary:
Bangladesh is a dangerous destination for trans visitors, with escalating Islamist violence since the August 2024 political crisis that ousted Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina. Trans activist Shila was brutally murdered in February 2025 (police suspect extremist involvement). A human-rights group documented 260 anti-LGBTQI+ incidents in 2024 — including murder, arson, and blackmail — describing attacks as having "skyrocketed." Islamist fundamentalist groups have intensified attacks under the interim government, and LGBTQ+ people have been "forced into hiding." A mob stormed the gate of a safe house for third-gender people (one survivor said "I escaped only with my life").

Police extort hijra/trans people — dozens were arrested for refusing to pay extortion money, and five were arrested at Dhaka's international airport.

The US State Department rates Bangladesh as Level 3 (Reconsider Travel).
visible.tangentialFactors: Same-sex conduct is criminalised under colonial-era Section 377 (life imprisonment, "rarely enforced" but used by police for harassment and extortion) — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active.
visible.localsOnly: Hijra people are legally recognised as a third gender (2013/2014, a genuine positive), but there is no anti-discrimination law and no comprehensive legal gender recognition — resident-facing framework.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Political instability, mob violence/lynchings, terrorism, and cyclone/monsoon risks affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

sources.claim: Erasing 76 Crimes (12 Feb 2025): prominent trans advocate Shila, originally from Chattogram district, was murdered in her home in Betbunia, Rangamati district on 3 Feb 2025; five unidentified individuals accused; she was widely known for humanitarian work. For this record: lethal violence against visible trans people continues — case specifics (Rangamati, Feb 2025).

Erasing 76 Crimes (7 Apr 2026) citing JMBF's annual report: 260 documented human-rights violations affecting at least 426 LGBTQI+ individuals nationwide in 2025 — 'a sharp increase' continuing an upward trend since 2022 — including murder/attempted murder, assault, abduction, arbitrary arrest, fabricated charges and extortion. For this record: the current national incident baseline — magnitude and trend for a visitor assessing exposure.

Global Press Journal: after the 2024 Monsoon Revolution, hardline conservative Islamist groups gained ground; Bangladesh has officially recognised third-gender identity since 2013 (a rural town elected a trans woman mayor in 2021), but trans lives have been upended — the featured subject now lives in hiding. For this record: the 2024 regime-change inflection point where formal rights began rolling back in practice.

Washington Blade (5 Aug 2025): a year after protests forced Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina's ouster (August 2024), Bangladesh's LGBTQ community is increasingly vulnerable to violence amid Islamist mobilisation and threats. For this record: a dated, post-coup security assessment directly relevant to a visitor's risk calculus.

UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity, Bangladesh (September 2023, updated April 2026): Section 377 ambiguity persists — it remains unclear whether lesbianism falls within s.377 (ILGA's 2019 State-Sponsored Homophobia report read female-female activity as not criminal while elsewhere calling the provision relevant to 'all genders'). For this record: authoritative statement of the legal ambiguity any visitor's conduct sits inside.

Outright International (updated 12 Mar 2026): Penal Code 1860 criminalises 'intercourse against the order of nature' with up to life imprisonment — rarely enforced but used by police to harass people presumed LGBTIQ; hijra are legally recognised as a third gender since 2014 with gender-marker change allowed; LGBTIQ and hijra pride events have been held. For this record: the legal baseline plus the harassment-not-prosecution enforcement pattern and third-gender recognition.

Erasing 76 Crimes (22 Oct 2025): after hijras refused police extortion money on 10 Sep 2025, at least twelve were injured in a retaliatory attack in Gomdondi Phultala; on 17 Sep police arrested twelve hijras collecting money from expatriate-carrying vehicles in Narayanganj — a traditional livelihood. For this record: extortion-driven police violence against visibly trans people, including disruption of street livelihoods.

Erasing 76 Crimes (22 Apr 2024): five transgender/hijra women were arrested while begging near Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka and sentenced to about a month in custody, per JMBF. For this record: policing of visibly trans people concentrates at transit hubs — the airport itself is a documented hotspot.

UK Upper Tribunal decision PA/07096/2017 (Feb 2019): a Bangladeshi gay man's asylum appeal — Home Office country material records Islamist groups calling to prosecute LGBT people under Section 377 and Sharia, threats against LGBT journalists, and a government that does not recognise LGBT issues (citing fact-finding missions and IRB Canada). For this record: asylum-grade evidence of state-tolerated hostility; international-regime (asylum) source in scope by design.

visible.summary:
Uganda is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. The 2023 Anti-Homosexuality Act imposes life imprisonment for same-sex conduct and the death penalty for "aggravated homosexuality," and the US State Department explicitly warns that "the law applies to both visitors and residents." Over 1,000 rights violations (arrests, torture, evictions) were documented in nine months. Mobs have gathered outside trans people's homes (one woman described being grabbed and shouted at that she needed to die); police use digital entrapment (obtaining evidence via dating apps); and the government has "spread misinformation and hatred against LGBT people." The law also criminalises the "promotion of homosexuality," meaning any advocacy or support is banned.

There are no laws regulating gender identity — the AHA targets same-sex conduct and promotion, not trans identity per se — but trans people are swept up in the broader anti-LGBT crackdown, mobs, and state violence. The Constitutional Court upheld the AHA in April 2024 (striking down only a few provisions on healthcare access and renting).

Uganda's death penalty is for "aggravated" same-sex (not all same-sex like Iran; not gender expression per se like Saudi), and no trans-specific visitor killing or border-targeting is documented — but the systematic state-led crackdown makes this a environment to avoid entirely.
visible.tangentialFactors: The AHA's life imprisonment and "aggravated homosexuality" death penalty apply to visitors — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active; dating-app entrapment is a direct app-user risk.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Terrorism (ADF in border areas), violent crime (armed robbery, sexual assault), and civil unrest affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch report 'They're Putting Our Lives at Risk' (26 May 2025): Uganda's 2023 Anti-Homosexuality Act — death penalty for 'aggravated homosexuality', lengthy prison terms for 'promotion of homosexuality' — unleashed arrests, shelter raids, evictions and public outings; many LGBT people in hiding, with a small group of Ugandan mothers speaking publicly for their LGBT children.

Human Rights Watch (4 Apr 2024): Uganda's Constitutional Court upheld the 2023 Anti-Homosexuality Act's core provisions — including the death penalty in certain circumstances and penalties up to 20 years — rejecting public-participation challenges; contrasted with the same court voiding a similar 2013 law on procedure.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying Reuters report (June 2024) covers rights violations against Uganda's LGBTQ community escalating, per a pressure group.

The Guardian (7 Jan 2024): fear across Kampala after the anti-gay laws — a transgender woman mobbed and beaten into a two-week coma after a false TikTok allegation, sheltering with 20 others at a Kampala safe house; notes the death penalty for 'aggravated homosexuality', international condemnation, and continued political support for the law in parts of Africa.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying US State Department travel advisory for Uganda includes LGBT-specific warnings under the 'Do Not Travel' advisory.

Access Now (15 May 2025): Uganda's anti-LGBTQ+ laws are used to entrap people online — digital entrapment is one of the main tactics authorities use against LGBTQ+ people via apps, while the companies behind popular apps do too little; shares 2025 case research and safety recommendations — directly relevant to visitor device/app risk under the AHA.

Amnesty International (23 Oct 2024) report 'Everybody Here Is Having Two Lives or Names': the devastating impact of criminalisation on digital spaces for LGBTQ people in Uganda — widespread technology-facilitated gender-based violence (doxxing, impersonation, hacking, disinformation); the AHA 2023 fostered a climate of impunity forcing people and organisations to alter how they present themselves online.

AP (Feb 2026): 'Ugandan police arrest two women for allegedly kissing in public' — two women detained in Arua after neighbours reported them; one of the first known arrests under the 2023 Anti-Homosexuality Act.

US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Uganda: the three most important problems included 'violence and discrimination against marginalized groups (women...; children...; persons with disabilities; and the lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender community)' - the era of the Anti-Homosexuality Bill debates.

visible.summary:
Egypt is a dangerous destination for trans visitors — with a directly documented study on the treatment of queer foreigners by Egyptian authorities ("Your Kind Is Not Welcome Here," Cairo 52, 12 incidents 2018-2022). Same-sex conduct is not explicitly criminalised, but authorities use "debauchery" and cybercrime laws (six months + fine for "violation of social and family values") to arrest and prosecute — and courts have moved from de facto to explicit criminalisation under the cybercrime law.

Police hunt LGBT people on dating apps (BBC Grindr entrapment) and subject arrestees to coerced anal examinations. Gender-affirming healthcare is prohibited. The Ministry of Interior is closing a loophole that allowed limited legal gender recognition. Egypt rejected all UN recommendations on sexual orientation and gender identity in its 2025 Universal Periodic Review. The authorities' approach is described as "not only to criminalize LGBTQ+ identities but also to erase them from society and public life."

Egypt has no death penalty for same-sex (unlike Uganda/Nigeria's death penalties), no documented trans-specific tourist killing, and the statutory penalty is six months + fine (not 14 years or life) — but the systematic police entrapment, foreigner-targeting, coerced anal exams, and healthcare prohibition make the practical risk severe.
visible.tangentialFactors: Dating-app entrapment (BBC Grindr case) is a direct risk for trans visitors using apps; the debauchery/cybercrime statutes also capture same-sex conduct.
visible.localsOnly: The gender-affirming healthcare prohibition and the closure of the limited LGR loophole are resident-facing.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Terrorism (Sinai), political instability, and general crime affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

sources.claim: Cairo 52, 'Your Kind Is Not Welcome Here' (27 Nov 2023): analysis of Egypt's immigration law and case law plus 12 documented incidents (2018-2022) — Ministry of Interior holds broad powers to deny entry or deport anyone 'disturbing public order and morality', applied to travellers perceived as queer. Directly visitor-facing risk.

Cairo 52 (24 Jan 2024): Egypt's Economic Courts have moved from de-facto to EXPLICIT criminalisation by reading Penal Code provisions together with Art. 9(C) of the Anti-Sex Work Law 10/1961; Court of Cassation 1970s interpretations had already removed the financial-exchange requirement (habitual/multiple partners sufficed).

Cairo 52 (12 Dec 2024): a new Ministry of Interior directive to civil-registry heads nationwide closes the Civil Status Law 143/1994 loophole that let transgender Egyptians correct gender markers via governorate committees — legal gender recognition now actively being shut.

BBC investigation, 'How Egyptian police hunt LGBT people on dating apps': no explicit law against homosexuality, but the 'debauchery' (sex-work) law is used to criminalise the community; police run entrapment via apps with victims describing blackmail and arrests (names changed).

Bedayaa, '10 FAQs about LGBTIQs Situation in Egypt' (Feb 2023): documents rising arrests of homosexuals and trans people alongside coerced anal examinations, authorities turning a blind eye, and no anti-discrimination policy or law; covers detention conditions and the trans situation as a reference for SOGIESC work.

EIPR security documentation: police arrest patterns — first, entrapment of individuals, especially transgender women, through fake accounts on LGBTQ dating apps and websites; second, Ministry of Interior deportation of foreign nationals suspected of being gay or trans even without charges upheld; violations continue inside police stations.

Outright country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): homosexuality not explicitly criminalised, yet vague public-morality and debauchery laws are routinely used for arrests carrying prison sentences; NO legal protection against discrimination on sexual orientation, gender identity, expression or sex characteristics.

TIMEP (6 Jan 2025): for Egypt's fourth UPR cycle — transgender and intersex Egyptians face discriminatory laws, policies and practices violating the right to health; barriers to equitable health services persist since the last UPR, with pervasive gender-identity and sexual-orientation discrimination in healthcare.

Human Rights Watch, 'In a Time of Torture: The Assault on Justice in Egypt's Crackdown on Homosexual Conduct' (29 Feb 2004): documents the Queen Boat-era crackdown — arbitrary arrests, dark cells and beatings over sexual orientation, with testimony from defendants — the landmark record of state violence against gay men in Egypt.

visible.summary:
Uruguay is one of Latin America's safest and most progressive destinations for trans visitors. The Comprehensive Law for Trans People (Law 19,684, 2018) provides legal gender recognition by administrative self-declaration (no surgery or diagnosis required), a reparation pension for trans victims of institutional violence, and a state employment quota for trans people. Same-sex marriage has been legal since 2013 (Latin America's first), and bathroom access is legally protected.

The country is consistently ranked among Latin America's safest (Global Peace Index), with a "strong democratic governance structure and positive record of upholding political rights and civil liberties" (Freedom House). However, a 29-year-old trans woman, Joana, was shot dead in her home in Montevideo in July 2025 (the assailant was sentenced to 7 years), and discrimination incidents have been documented at a hospital (San Carlos) and a bank (BROU). Freedom House notes "disparities in treatment" for transgender people despite legal equality.

For a visitor: no border friction, bathrooms protected, no criminalisation, and Montevideo is welcoming.
visible.tangentialFactors: Same-sex marriage legal since 2013 (Latin America's first) — relevant to trans visitors travelling with partners.
visible.localsOnly: The self-declaration LGR, reparation pension, and state employment quota under Law 19,684 are resident-facing; the Joana killing and the hospital/bank discrimination incidents concerned residents.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: General crime is very low; no trans-specific travel advisory.

sources.claim: Outright country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex relations legal nationwide, legal gender recognition possible, LGBTI orgs registrable; intersex bodily-autonomy protections flagged incomplete. The current civil-rights baseline a trans visitor enters.

Full text of Law No. 19684 (26 Oct 2018), Uruguay's Comprehensive Law for Trans People: state-guaranteed identity, health and anti-discrimination rights for trans persons -- the statutory backbone of the country's trans-protection regime.

Equaldex status grid for Montevideo (governed by national law): marriage, legal gender change, non-discrimination, conversion-therapy ban and equal age of consent all legal/protected; hate-crime rules cover SOGI. Compiled status page, undated.
Presidencia release: the Executive promulgated the Comprehensive Law for Trans Persons (Ley 19684, Oct 2018) -- official confirmation the comprehensive trans-rights statute entered into force.
Freedom House Uruguay 2024: Free, 96/100 (political rights 40/40, civil liberties 56/60) -- strong general rights climate for trans visitors.

TDoR 2025 record: Joana, a 29-year-old trans woman, shot dead in her Montevideo home on 28 Jul 2025; a suspect was subsequently sentenced to 7 years for the murder -- documented lethal violence against a trans person with judicial follow-through.

la diaria (May 2024): trans health-service user Andreina Stuart denounced mistreatment and discrimination at San Carlos hospital (Maldonado); criminal complaint pending, hospital director pledged an administrative investigation after the judicial stage; local officials pressed for health-system updates.

Beccah Rivas, a trans woman, sued state bank BROU over discriminatory handling by a Prosegur guard and alleges the bank withheld the key camera footage; prosecutor Tania Vidal compelled the bank to produce material; Rivas says she was dismissed after publicising the case.

PinkNews (28 Dec 2007): Uruguay became the first Latin American country to recognise same-sex civil unions -- President Tabare Vazquez signed the law giving couples cohabiting 5+ years rights equivalent to marriage (historical baseline).

visible.summary:
Sri Lanka is dangerous for trans visitors. Sections 365/365A of the 1883 Penal Code criminalise same-sex activity (up to 10 years, applying to men and women), and Human Dignity Trust lists Sri Lanka as criminalising the gender expression of trans people: police use vagrancy and “cheating by personation” provisions against trans people. The International Commission of Jurists identifies Sri Lanka Police as “the foremost perpetrators of human rights violations against LGBTI individuals” — harassment, arbitrary detention, and abuse are documented as systematic, though formal prosecutions remain limited.

There is no legal gender recognition (a 2016 recognition circular exists but is not law), no anti-discrimination protection, and no hate-crime statute. Colombo has a small organised community (EQUAL GROUND) and tourist areas are accustomed to foreigners, which moderates but does not remove risk: the realistic worst case is police harassment or detention under personation/vagrancy provisions rather than prosecution.
visible.tangentialFactors: Sections 365/365A criminalise same-sex activity (up to 10 years) — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners; the vagrancy and "personation" provisions are the trans-specific enforcement vehicle.
visible.localsOnly: The 2016 recognition circular (not law) is a resident-facing instrument.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Same-sex criminalisation is a situational/climate factor; LGR circular limits are resident-facing.

sources.claim: Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): Sections 365/365A of the Penal Code criminalise same-sex activity (up to 10 years, applying to men and women); prosecutions limited but harassment, violence, extortion, arbitrary arrests and denial of services are frequent; no comprehensive anti-discrimination protections; authorities use forced anal and vaginal examinations to seek evidence - widely condemned as torture. Legal gender recognition is possible (via a certification process).
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Human Dignity Trust country profile documents Sri Lanka's criminalisation of same-sex activity.

ICJ opinion piece (Aug 2023) by Mathuri Thamilmaran: 'Protecting transgender persons: Going beyond rule by circular' - the Sri Lanka Police are the foremost perpetrators of human-rights violations against LGBTI individuals; recent months saw both the Police and the Human Rights Commission acknowledging this; argues administrative circulars are insufficient without legal reform.

UK Home Office CPIN Sri Lanka: Sexual orientation and gender identity or expression (v6.0, Sept 2024): assessment of risk from state and non-state actors, protection, internal relocation and certification for LGBT+ asylum claims, with detailed country information.

US State Department country report for Sri Lanka (custom URL): official human-rights assessment including the SOGI section - criminalisation under the penal code and police harassment of LGBT persons.

Joint UPR stakeholder report (EQUAL GROUND, Northwestern CIHR, GIHR) for Sri Lanka's 3rd cycle: 'Human Rights Violations Against LGBTIQ Individuals in Sri Lanka' - documents criminalisation and violations by the coalition of NGOs for UPR.

Canada IRB Response to Information Request LKA103948.E (Jan 2012): 'Treatment of sexual minorities in Sri Lanka' - Article 365 criminalises 'carnal intercourse against the order of nature' (up to 10 years, men only); Article 365A 'gross indecency' (both sexes, amended 1995 to cover women); rarely enforced with no convictions, but criminalisation 'paves the way for police and anti-gay groups to brand all lesbian, bisexual, transgendered persons as perverts and criminals'.
